title: Stasimon 5 (lines 1054–1093)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus calls on Dionysus, Thebes' own god, to come and heal the city. Hope rises just before the catastrophe, a tragic pattern that also appears in Oedipus Rex.

Of a Theban bride the wonder,

Dionysus, thou art seen.

Strophe 1
Thou by many names adored,
Child of Zeus the God of thunder,
Of a Theban bride the wonder,
Fair Italia’s guardian lord;
In the deep-embosomed glades
Of the Eleusinian Queen
Haunt of revellers, men and maids,
Dionysus, thou art seen.
Where Ismenus rolls his waters,
Where the Dragon’s teeth were sown,
Where the Bacchanals thy daughters
Round thee roam,

All hall to thee
Evoë, Evoë!

Authentic son of Zeus, immortal king,

I read “Thou by many names adored, / Child of Zeus the God of thunder, / Of a Theban bride the wonder, / Fair Italia’s guardian lord; / In the deep-embosomed glades / Of the Eleusinian Queen / Haunt of revellers, men and maids, / Dionysus, thou art seen.” slowly and put it in my own words: The elders call on Dionysus by his many titles: son of Zeus and a Theban bride, guardian of Italy, a god seen among revellers in the glades of Eleusis. Next, craft. I notice the song is a hymn: it piles up titles and places to summon the god. The strongest word is “Dionysus”: Thebes' own god and the god of the theatre. Then, effect. Why do the elders call on Dionysus, the god of Thebes, at this point in the play? My answer: The elders call on Dionysus at this point because they hope Creon's change of heart has saved the city and want its own god to come and heal it; the hymn's joy is a false dawn before the messenger's news.
